`KloEntity[]` - Array of all dependent entities including the newly added one

Adds a dependent entity to be included in the data message sent to endpoints. Dependent entities are additional entities that should be sent along with the main entity object. This is useful when you need to send related data that may not be directly linked but is contextually important.

```ts
let endpointBean = eventContext.addEndpoint("USER001", EndpointType.USER, ChannelType.DEVICE, orderEntity);
let customerEntity = await txn.loadEntityP("d_customer", customerKey);
endpointBean.addDependantEntities(customerEntity); // Customer info sent along with order
```


chunks.t: Application not working or private node screen not displaying
chunks.x:
**Q: Why is my application not working, and why isn't the private node screen in VS Code displaying as expected?**

**A:** If you encounter issues with the application not working, follow these steps:

- Open Command Prompt and type **ipconfig** to check your current IP address.

- Compare the IP address displayed with the one maintained in the hosts file.

- If the IP address in the hosts file does not match the current IP, update the hosts file with the correct IP address.

- After saving the changes, restart the application and check if the issue is resolved.

- This will help ensure that the correct IP address is mapped for proper application functionality.

chunks.t: Port number must match the private URL
chunks.x:
**Q: Why is it important for the port number in the private node server to match the port number in the private URL when opening the application in the browser?**

**A:** It is crucial for the port number in the private node server to match the port number in the private URL because:

1.  The port number in the URL defines which specific service or application on the server is being accessed.

2.  If the port numbers don't match, the browser will attempt to connect to the wrong service, potentially resulting in an error or failure to load the application correctly.

3.  Ensuring that both the server configuration and the private URL use the same port number guarantees proper communication and accessibility between the client (browser) and the server.

4.  Mismatched port numbers can lead to incorrect routing or connection failures, preventing the application from loading as expected after selecting the **"Open Application in Browser"** option.

**Note**: Always verify that the port number shown in the URL matches the one configured on the server to avoid connectivity issues.

chunks.t: JavaScript heap out of memory with tsc -w
chunks.x:
**Q: I'm getting a "JavaScript heap out of memory" / "FATAL ERROR: Ineffective mark-compacts near heap limit" error when running tsc -w in Private Node. What's causing this and how do I fix it?**

**A:** This typically happens when your system doesn't have enough free RAM left for the TypeScript watcher to allocate memory — often because browsers (Chrome/Edge) or other applications are already consuming most of the available memory. On an 8GB machine, it's common to see 7GB+ already in use before the compiler even starts.

**Immediate fix:**

- Close unused browser tabs/windows and other memory-heavy applications before starting a tsc -w session.

Alternatively, give Node a defined heap budget so it fails more gracefully or succeeds where the default limit was too aggressive:
set NODE_OPTIONS=--max-old-space-size=4096 tsc -w

-

**If the issue persists or recurs frequently:**

- A RAM upgrade (16GB recommended) is advised for machines regularly running Private Node builds alongside browsers/IDEs.

- Check that tsconfig.json includes incremental: true and skipLibCheck: true to reduce the compiler's memory footprint per rebuild.

- Use cmd terminal to start the typescript watcher (tsc -w).

- For a fresh system if an application wants to create all their tables by using the installation screen then **t_schema_def** is not required to be maintained.

App Mover is a standalone application resource.

**Step 1:** In the portal’s menu tab, go to **Admin Center**.

**Step 2:** Under Admin Center select **Advanced Migration**. You will be taken to the installation screen.

A preview of the Installation Screen is given below:

The installation screen is used to install or update external apps. This includes the app’s folder that will be saved in the closedmodules folder and its zip will be extracted in cdn_app. Apart from this, the installation screen does the following tasks in the background:

- Update **madm_app** table.

- Update the Flavor folder in the closedmodules folder.

- Update the Flavor zip in the **cdn_app** folder.

- Create/Update Tables for that App and its dependent app.

- Install Config for that App.

The screen will have a table which contains all information relevant to the app.

Following is a list of columns in the app installation screen like the App name.

| **Components**    | **Description**                                                                                                                                         |

| **App**           | Name of the app.                                                                                                                                        |
| **BOL Version**   | BOL version used by the app.                                                                                                                            |
| **Version**       | A version of the app.                                                                                                                                   |
| **Is External**   | It is a component of the app. If **is_external** is marked as false then the app is in closedmodules, if marked as true then the app is in **cdn_app**. |
| **Dependant App** | Shows the dependent app information of a particular app with the dependent app name and version.                                                        |
| **Created On**    | Shows the date app was created.                                                                                                                         |
| **Landscape**     | The landscape where the apps are present.                                                                                                               |

To install an app follow the following steps:

1.  Click the **Upload App** button on the top left of the screen to select the zip file and press OK.
    > **Note:** zip name should be proper for eg:- **app_version.zip**.

>

2.  Then a popup screen will appear that will give relevant details related to the app, if the app is already there in the **madm_app** table then it will ask for an **install**. If it's not there then it will ask for an **update**.

>

3.  On click of install or update, **madm_app** will be updated, tables for that app will be generated and the app zip will be placed inside closed modules with extracted files.

There is one download button that lets you download any app‘s zip from the current server (**cdn_app**) where the application is running.

>

**Note:-**

- If the app is internal (i.e. r_is_external = 0), it will be downloaded from the cdn_app/release_build folder (i.e. prodBuild zip).

- If the app is external (i.e. r_is_external = 1), it will be downloaded from the cdn_app folder (i.e. devBuild zip).

- Whenever you make any changes in an existing app that has already been moved using the Advanced app mover; You need to change the app version make the changes in the app and then move the app. This will help in triggering the Update Schema through the URL. chunks.x:
A **.certSigningRequest** file is a critical part of the **certificate generation process** in iOS development. It is used to create a **code-signing certificate**, which is necessary for signing your iOS apps for distribution via **In-House** or **Ad Hoc** methods. The CSR file contains information about the developer or the organization, including the public key, which is used by Apple to generate the appropriate signing certificate.If you want to create a new **Certificate,** then follow the steps below.

- Open the keychain Access as shown in the below screenshot.

>

- Click on **Request a Certificate From a Certificate Authority** as shown in the below screenshot.

>

- Click on **Keychain Access** as shown in the below screenshot.

>

- Fill the below details as shown in the below screenshot.

  - The user's email address plays an indirect role in the code-signing process since it is linked to your Apple Developer account and included in the signing certificate's metadata. While the Keychain holds the signing certificate and private key, it does not store the email address in plain text. Instead, the email is embedded within the certificate's metadata, which identifies the developer or organization.

  - **In short:**

- Email is used to identify the developer in the signing certificate.

  - The **CA Email Address** is a part of the Issuer information within a certificate and provides a way to contact the Certificate Authority that issued the certificate. It serves as a point of contact for issues related to the certificate, such as validation, renewal, or revocation. You can find the CA's email address in the certificate metadata, which can be inspected in various tools like Keychain Access on macOS or by viewing the certificate details in a web browser.

chunks.h: 2.1. Create a Certificates for your Project > 2.1.2.Certificate the Certificates
chunks.x:
- **Certificates** ensure your app is properly authorized for development, testing, and distribution. They act as a security mechanism to ensure that only authorized developers and apps can interact with Apple devices. Without these certificates, your app cannot be installed on devices or distributed via the App Store.

- If you want to create a new **Certificate,** then follow the steps below.

1.  Open your Apple developer account.

2.  Click on **Certificates** as shown in the below screenshot

>

3.  Click on the **create ( + )** button as shown below.

>

4.  Select the **In-House and Ad Hoc** check box and click on **continue.**

> **In-House**: Choose this if you need to distribute apps internally within a company, especially if the app is for internal use and will be installed on many devices within your organization. This is the best choice for enterprise-level apps and internal tools.
>
> **Ad Hoc**: Choose Ad Hoc distribution if you have a small group of testers or specific clients who need to test or review your app before release. This is the best choice for beta testing or distributing an app to a limited number of users.
>
> **Both methods are critical for scenarios where an app is not intended for public release via the App Store but needs to be tested or used by a controlled group.**
>
>

5.  In the next screen select the certificate request file (a file with a **.certSigningRequest** file extension), then click Choose and click on continue.

6.  Now you can see the Certificate in the list as shown below,

>

- The **Bundle ID** is a unique identifier for your iOS app, and its uses in app development and distribution are crucial for various processes:

  - **App Identification**: Differentiates your app from others in the Apple ecosystem and **App Store**.

  - **Code Signing and Provisioning Profiles**: Ties the app to **provisioning profiles** for code signing.

  - **Enabling Services**: Used to enable services like **Push Notifications**, **iCloud**, **In-App Purchases**, **Game Center**, and more.

  - **Managing Versions**: Helps to manage different versions of the app, such as production and staging.

  - **App Group and Keychain Sharing**: Facilitates data sharing between multiple apps.

  - **App Distribution**: Ensures correct signing and submission for **App Store** or **TestFlight**.

  - **App Extensions**: Ties extensions (e.g., widgets, share extensions) to the main app.

  - **Security**: Ensures app integrity during installation and distribution.

- If you want to create a new **key** then follow the steps below.

1.  Click the ( + ) button to create a new key as shown below.

>

2.  Fill in the **key name** field and select the APN service, then click the **Continue** button.

>

3.  Click the **Register** button to continue as shown below.

>

4.  **Copy the key** **ID**, download the APN auth key and then click on the **Done** button to complete the process.

5.  You can check the new key in your key list as shown below:

chunks.t: Restrict Save Operation on Compilation Failure in VS Code Extension
chunks.x:
When saving a single file, if any compilation errors are detected, a warning message will appear: **'Errors found during compilation. Do you still wish to commit?'**

Warning message will have the following options:

2.  **Show Errors**: Clicking this option will display the compilation errors that were detected in the output channel.

3.  **Cancel**:Aborts the current action.

When the server environment moves to a newer Klobase (Procify Framework) version, your existing Private Node workspace can now be updated in place. You no longer need a new folder and a new Private Node for every Klobase update. Your checked-out apps, uncommitted changes under src and pending-change tracking stay exactly as they are.

Note: The feature is available post klobase 7-2-365 and later version and Procifynow IDE 7.0.25 and later versions, Working on an older version will not allow the feature

chunks.h: 8.2. Klobase Update in the Same Workspace > How to Update
chunks.x:
1.  When a new Klobase version is detected, the **Klobase Update Required** tab opens in VS Code. It shows the **Current Workspace**, the **Previous Klobase Version** and the **New Klobase Version**. *(Figure 1)*

2.  Any app changes that came with the update are listed under **Application changes in this update**. They are grouped as *Updated*, *Added*, *Removed*, *Write access granted* and *Write access removed*. Each group expands and collapses, and long lists scroll.

3.  Click **Update in This Workspace** (the recommended option). The button shows *Updating...* while it runs.

4.  The Private Node restarts once, automatically. Keep VS Code open until it finishes.

5.  A notification confirms the new version, for example *“Procify Framework updated from 7-2-364 to 7-2-365 in this workspace.”*, and the tab closes. *(Figure 2)*

You can also start it from the Command Palette: **Update Procify Framework in This Workspace**.

**What Is Kept:** checked-out apps, uncommitted changes under src (the notification says how many were left untouched), and pending-change tracking.

chunks.h: 8.2. Klobase Update in the Same Workspace > If Something Goes Wrong
chunks.x:
| **Message**                                                           | **What happened**                                                                                      | **What to do**                               |

| *Framework update failed: ... restored to its previous version*       | It failed before the new version was applied. The workspace and node are back on the previous version. | Retry, or use **Start in a new workspace**.  |
| *Framework updated to X, but the app list could not be refreshed ...* | The new version is applied and the node is running on it. Only the app refresh failed.                 | Run **Update Apps** once the node is up.     |
| *This workspace runs Klobase X, which cannot be updated in place ...* | This workspace’s Klobase build doesn’t support in-place updates.                                       | Use **Start in a new workspace**, as before. |

**Note:** **Start in a new workspace** (**Continue in New Workspace**) is still available. Uncommitted changes stay in the old folder and have to be copied across by hand.
**Note:** In-place updates require the matching Procify IDE extension build.

If you encounter issues with the application not opening in the browser, follow these steps:

- Compare the IP address displayed with the one maintained in the hosts file.

- If the IP address in the hosts file does not match the current IP, update the hosts file with the correct IP address.

- This will help ensure that the correct IP address is mapped for proper application functionality.

Format per line: IP_address \ hostname [aliases...]
Example: 10.1.1.101 procifynowide.com

  > ip addr show or short ip a
  > or hostname -I for a quick list of IPs

chunks.x:
1.  Open terminal

2.  run command `cd /etc`

3.  Open the file hosts in vscode, by running the command `sudo code hosts`. This will ask for the password, after entering the password, it will open the file in vscode.

(If vs code is not opened, then continue from step ‘A’ mentioned below).

4.  Update the hosts file with the mac's IP Address, It is possible that it(Macbook’s IP address) got changed.

5.  Update or add the IP Address of the server you want to connect to, as it is done on windows.

6.  Then save the file. There will be a pop up asking to use sudo access.

7.  Click on *Retry as sudo **

8.  Input the password as prompted. Then Press OK. This will save the file.**

If above steps not working then

1.  Open terminal and run the command `sudo nano /etc/hosts`. This will ask for the password, after entering the password, It will shows hosts Ip list.

2.  Use arrow keys to move the pointer to the particular IDE ip and change it with current ip.

3.  To save the changes, use `Ctrl + O` then press `Enter`.

4.  Then press `Ctrl + X` to exit the nano.

chunks.h: Private Node Setup on Macbook — Node Modules
chunks.x:
Right now node modules are not installed globally.

So you have to install them manually(Copy the existing node_modules folder to your private node folder). In the MacBook, currently, node modules are installed in the folder `Documents/PrivateNode`.

chunks.h: Private Node Setup on Macbook — Where to find the VSIX
chunks.x: VSIX is installed in VSCode already. If not, then take it from the extension owner and install the VSIX.

chunks.t: How to set up Private Node
chunks.h: Private Node Setup on Macbook — How to set up Private Node > Steps
chunks.x:
1.  Open the folder `Documents/PrivateNode` in the Finder.

2.  Create a new folder.

3.  Open that folder in vscode.

4.  A WebView will open. If not,***

> Activate the extension by

- Press cmd+shift+p

- Search **Procifynow: Procify Version Selection**

- Press Enter

5.  Add the url to the prompt, and press ***Next***.****

6.  Then a new Screen will open.

7.  Input the Username and Password there.

8.  And hit ***Start Setup***.*****

9.  The Private Node should be set up normally.

**Developer Level 2 — Advanced Track**

*Enhancing the Customer Complaints Application*

This track does not build a new application. Every session goes back into the SAME Customer Complaints app built in Developer Level 1, and layers a new advanced capability onto it — the same end-to-end build approach used in the Level 1 guide.

**Prerequisite: Developer Level 1 completion is mandatory.**

*Proposed dates are placeholders (one session per working day, starting Mon 07 Sep 2026) — confirm actual start date and cadence.*

Developer Level 1 was built as an end-to-end project: one real application — the Customer Complaints Application — built up session by session. This Level 2 guide follows the same approach: no new application is created. Every session below re-opens the entities, pages, entity files, and controllers already built in Level 1 and extends them with an advanced capability, so trainees see how real applications evolve rather than practicing features in isolation.

Topics are drawn from the Training Topics sheet, filtered to entries tagged “Developer Level 2,” and mapped onto concrete enhancements of the existing app. Tool names use the current naming glossary, with legacy names noted where relevant.

Sessions must be taken in order — each session's steps assume the previous session's enhancement is already in place, exactly as in the Level 1 guide.

| Session | Date | Topic Area | Application Enhancement |

| **Session 1** | Mon, 07 Sep 2026 | Advanced BOL & Data Modelling | Network Modes — Offline-Ready Properties · Sort Order & Entity Index · Entity Rules — Auto-Escalation on Update · Query Rules — Role-Based Field Masking · BOL Transaction — Close Complaint with Feedback |
| **Session 2** | Tue, 08 Sep 2026 | Advanced Page Builder & Client-Side Debugging | Embedded Section — Complaint Timeline · Advanced kloControls · TransNode onArrive & navigateId · Server-Side Debugging & Auto Update Data |
| **Session 3** | Wed, 09 Sep 2026 | Security, Permissions & Data Access | Design-Time Permissions · Row Wise Auth · Data Access Rules & User Access Summary · Role Permissions (Runtime) & Permission Logs |
| **Session 4** | Thu, 10 Sep 2026 | Offline, Middleware & Bulk Data | Local Archive · Initial Downloads · Middleware — Device & SAP · KloSectionXlsx — Bulk Customer Import |
| **Session 5** | Fri, 11 Sep 2026 | Workflows, Scheduling & Notifications | Escalation Approval Workflow · Scheduler — Nightly SLA Sweep · Notifications · deeplink & Banner |
| **Session 6** | Mon, 14 Sep 2026 | Reporting — Charts & Pivot Modeller | kloChart — Status Breakdown · Advanced Chart — TAT Trend · Pivot Modeller |
| **Session 7** | Tue, 15 Sep 2026 | Monitoring & Troubleshooting | Scheduler & Log Monitoring · Notification & Queue Monitoring · APK/IPA & Query Console |
| **Session 8** | Wed, 16 Sep 2026 | App Management, Branding & Deployment | App Inheritance & Modification · Customer Branding · Git Repo & Active Sessions · App Migration to QA |

chunks.h: Session 1 — Advanced BOL & Data Modelling > Session Objectives
chunks.x:
* Configure Network Modes so offline-relevant properties sync correctly to field devices.
* Apply Sort Order and an Entity Index to `d_complaints` for performance and predictable ordering.
* Extend the existing Entity Rules with a new auto-escalation rule.
* Extend the existing Query Rules with role-based field masking.
* Build a BOL Transaction that commits two entities atomically.

:::info What This Session Builds On
Developer Level 1 (Sessions 1–5) built `d_complaints` with its properties, one Entity Rule (`onCreateComplaint`) and one Query Rule (`beforeQ`) on `q_complaints`. This session does not start a new entity — it goes back into the same `d_complaints` and `q_complaints` files and adds the advanced BOL capabilities on top.
:::

chunks.h: Session 1 — Advanced BOL & Data Modelling > Session Objectives > Scenario
chunks.x: A field IT Team member on a tablet needs complaint status and priority visible even with no signal, while internal notes stay server-side only. Meanwhile complaints are quietly sailing past SLA with no auto-flag, and a support rep spots that anyone on the IT Team can see a customer's full contact details in the list — details they never needed for their job.

chunks.h: Session 1 — Advanced BOL & Data Modelling > Session Objectives > Part A — Network Modes — Offline-Ready Properties
chunks.x:
*Not every property should sync to a field device the same way. Configure Network Mode per property on `d_complaints`.*

| # | Action | Detail |

| **1** | **Open properties** | Procify Data Studio → `d_complaints` → Properties tab. |
| **2** | **Restrict remark** | Set Network Mode = Online Only on `remark` — internal notes should not be cached on IT Team field devices. |
| **3** | **Always sync core fields** | Set Network Mode = Always on `complaint_id`, `s_status`, `priority` so they remain visible even when the device is offline. |
| **4** | **Save & update schema** | Save, then Update Schema, and confirm no errors. |

chunks.h: Session 1 — Advanced BOL & Data Modelling > Session Objectives > Part B — Sort Order & Entity Index
chunks.x:
*The complaints list currently has no defined default order and no index for the fields it is filtered on most.*

| # | Action | Detail |

| **1** | **Set Sort Order** | On `priority`: custom order CRITICAL > HIGH > MEDIUM > LOW. On `created_on`: DESCENDING as the secondary sort. |
| **2** | **Create Entity Index** | Entity Index tab → Add → ID: `idx_complaint_status_priority` — fields: `s_status`, `priority`. |
| **3** | **Update Schema** | Update Schema and verify the index is listed under the entity's Test → Data Browser diagnostics. |

chunks.h: Session 1 — Advanced BOL & Data Modelling > Session Objectives > Part C — Entity Rules — Auto-Escalation on Update
chunks.x:
*Reopen the same `d_complaints.ts` file from Level 1 Session 5 and add a second rule alongside `onCreateComplaint`.*

| # | Action | Detail |

| **1** | **Register the rule** | Rule tab → Add → Event Type: On Update | Channel: Always on Server | Clazz: this | Invocation Method: `checkEscalation`. |
| **2** | **Implement checkEscalation** | If `s_status` is OPEN or INPROCESS and (today − `created_on`) > 3 days, set `is_escalated` = true. |
| **3** | **Test** | Backdate a test record's `created_on` in Data Browser to 4 days ago, save, and confirm `is_escalated` flips to true. |

chunks.h: Session 1 — Advanced BOL & Data Modelling > Session Objectives > Part D — Query Rules — Role-Based Field Masking
chunks.x:
*Extend `q_complaints.ts` — the same file where `beforeQ` was written in Level 1 Session 4 — with an `afterQ` rule.*

| # | Action | Detail |

| **1** | **Add afterQ** | Event Type: After Query. In the handler, if the requesting role is IT_TEAM, replace customer contact fields in each result row with ‘•••’. |
| **2** | **Test as IT Team** | Log in as `it_` — confirm customer contact fields are masked in the list. |
| **3** | **Test as Manager** | Log in as `mgr_` — confirm the same fields show full data. |

chunks.h: Session 1 — Advanced BOL & Data Modelling > Session Objectives > Part E — BOL Transaction — Close Complaint with Feedback
chunks.x:
*Combine a status update and a new voice record into one atomic operation.*

| # | Action | Detail |

| **1** | **Create the transaction** | Data Studio → new BOL Transaction `Tx_CloseWithFeedback`, covering `d_complaints` (update `s_status` = CLOSED) and `d_complaint_voices` (create feedback record). |
| **2** | **Wire the button** | Add a ‘Close with Feedback’ action on `s_detail_header` that commits both TransNodes through this transaction. |
| **3** | **Test atomicity** | Force the voice record to fail validation (e.g. leave it blank) and confirm the status change also rolls back — not just the voice record. |

:::tip Session 1 Checkpoint
* ✔ Network Modes verified in an offline emulation for at least 3 properties.
* ✔ `s_complaints` defaults to priority order; `idx_complaint_status_priority` exists and is used.
* ✔ `checkEscalation` rule fires correctly on a backdated test record.
* ✔ `afterQ` masks customer fields for IT_TEAM but not for Manager.
* ✔ `Tx_CloseWithFeedback` commits both entities together or rolls back together.
:::

**Enhancement delivered:** Extends the existing `d_complaints` / `q_complaints` files from Level 1 (not a new entity) with offline sync control, performance indexing, automatic SLA escalation, field-level data masking by role, and an atomic close-with-feedback commit.

chunks.h: Session 2 — Advanced Page Builder & Client-Side Debugging > Session Objectives
chunks.x:
* Build a reusable Embedded Section and use it on two different pages.
* Add Advanced kloControls (rating, file uploader) to the detail screen.
* Configure TransNode onArrive and navigateId behaviour.
* Debug the Session 1 server-side rule using Server-Side Debugging.

:::info What This Session Builds On
`p_complaints` was built manually in Level 1 Session 2 and styled in Session 6; `p_complaint_dashboard` was built in Session 5. Both existing pages are extended here — no new page is created from scratch.
:::

chunks.h: Session 2 — Advanced Page Builder & Client-Side Debugging > Session Objectives > Scenario
chunks.x: A Manager opens a complaint and has to hunt across screens to see whether this customer has complained before. A rep marks a complaint resolved but there's no way to capture how satisfied the customer actually was, or attach a photo of a damaged product without emailing it separately.

chunks.h: Session 2 — Advanced Page Builder & Client-Side Debugging > Session Objectives > Part A — Embedded Section — Complaint Timeline
chunks.x:

| # | Action | Detail |

| **1** | **Create the section** | New section `s_complaint_timeline` (screenType: timeline) bound to a TransNode combining voices and status-change history. |
| **2** | **Embed in detail** | In `pa_comp_details`, add a new section, mark it Embedded, and point its source to `s_complaint_timeline`. |
| **3** | **Reuse on dashboard** | Add the same embedded section to `p_complaint_dashboard` as a ‘Recent Activity’ panel — confirming true cross-page reuse. |

chunks.h: Session 2 — Advanced Page Builder & Client-Side Debugging > Session Objectives > Part B — Advanced kloControls
chunks.x:
*Add two controls that were not covered in Level 1's basic control set.*

| # | Action | Detail |

| **1** | **Add kloRating** | On `s_detail_header`, add a kloRating control bound to a new transient property `t_satisfaction_score`, visible only when `s_status` = CLOSED. |
| **2** | **Add kloFileUploader** | On the attachments section, add kloFileUploader bound to the `d_complaints_attachment` relation built in Level 1. |

chunks.h: Session 2 — Advanced Page Builder & Client-Side Debugging > Session Objectives > Part C — TransNode onArrive & navigateId
chunks.x:
*Make the detail screen smarter about what loads automatically and where links resolve to.*

| # | Action | Detail |

| **1** | **Configure onArrive** | On the detail TransNode, set onArrive to auto-load the 5 most recent related voices — no extra click required. |
| **2** | **Configure navigateId** | On the `ticket_id` link control, set navigateId so it always resolves to `pa_complaint_details`, whether clicked from `p_complaints` or the dashboard's embedded timeline. |

chunks.h: Session 2 — Advanced Page Builder & Client-Side Debugging > Session Objectives > Part D — Server-Side Debugging & Auto Update Data
chunks.x:

**Training Guide**

		**Beginner**

**Date of Issue: 2025**
**Target Audience: Application Developers, Trainees.**

*A Training Manual for application creation, knowledge and work reference.*

**Training Procedure**

Welcome to the Procify Developer Training. This section explains the overall structure of the course, how sessions are designed, and what is expected of you as a trainee. Read this before starting Session 1.

The training spans 8 sessions. Each session introduces a new layer of the platform — starting with setup and ending with publishing a fully working application. Sessions must be taken in order; each one builds directly on the previous.

| Session | Topic |

| Session 1 | Platform Setup & Account Management |
| Session 2 | BOL — Entity Fundamentals & Initial Pages |
| Session 3 | Entity Configuration (Relations, Object Types, Status, ID Series) |
| Session 4 | Value Helps & Queries |
| Session 5 | BOL Logic & Validations with dashboard creation |
| Session 6 | Bindings, Navigation & Styling |
| Session 7 | Controllers & Client-Side Behaviour |
| Session 8 | Menu Configuration & App Management, Versioning & Publishing |

This training does not teach concepts in isolation. You will build one real application — a Customer complaint system — across all 89 sessions. Every concept is introduced exactly when you need it to make the next part of that application work.

| Why this matters for you You will always know WHY you are doing each step, not just HOW. By Session 8 you will have a working application demonstrating every major platform capability. The application grows session by session — if you miss a step it will affect later sessions. When you encounter a similar situation on a real project, you will have a concrete reference point from training. |

* Attend each session with the previous session's assignment completed and verified.

* Follow steps in this guide during hands-on time — do not skip ahead.

* Ask questions during the Review & Q\&A phase, not during the trainer demonstration.

| The Application You Will Build This training guide uses a REAL application: the Customer complaints Application. You are not building a demo — you are building a production-ready application for delivery personnel. Every concept taught in every session is applied directly to build this application. By Session 9 you will have a fully working, published Delivery Agent Application. |

chunks.h: Session 1 — Platform Setup & Account Management > Part A — Understanding the Customer complaint Application > Application Purpose
chunks.x:
The Customer Complaints Application is a solution designed to manage customer complaints end-to-end across three personas:

• Log and track customer complaints with full lifecycle management.

• Route complaints from Employee → Manager → Responsible Team.

• Manage complaint line items, voice records, and file attachments.

• Monitor escalations, SLA (TAT), and resolution timelines.

• Provide dashboards per role so every user sees what they need.

chunks.h: Session 1 — Platform Setup & Account Management > Part A — Understanding the Customer complaint Application > Application Roles — Three Personas
chunks.x:
This application defines exactly three application roles, each mapped to a Procify role-rollup level for viewable and UI-Auth controls:

| Role ID | Business Name | Procify Role Rollup |

| Employee | Complaint Creator | Owner (s_role_rollup \= 10) |
| Manager | Complaint Assignor | Supervisor (s_role_rollup \= 20) |
| Responsible Team | Issue Resolver | Reviewer (s_role_rollup \= 30) |

| 📘 Role Precedence Rule Precedence is a number. Lower \= higher priority. Employee: precedence 3, Manager: precedence 2, ResponsibleTeam: precedence 1. This means if a user has multiple roles, the lower-precedence number overrides. Your developer account should be assigned Manager (precedence 2) for full access during testing. |

chunks.h: Session 1 — Platform Setup & Account Management > Part A — Understanding the Customer complaint Application > Complaint Status Flow
chunks.x:
The status lifecycle has 6 states. Each transition is triggered by a specific role:

| OPEN | INPROCESS | ON HOLD | RESOLVED | CLOSED | REOPEN |

| **↓** | **↓** | **↓** | **↓** | **↓** |  |
| *Triggered by* **Employee** | *Triggered by* **Manager / Responsible Team** | *Triggered by* **Responsible Team** | *Triggered by* **Responsible Team / Manager** | *Triggered by* **Manager / Employee** | *Triggered by* **Employee / Manager** |

| Status | Badge Colour / Meaning |

| OPEN | Blue — complaint logged by Employee, awaiting Manager assignment |
| INPROCESS | Orange — Manager assigned responsible team; team working on it |
| ON HOLD | Purple — Responsible Team placed on hold pending information |
| RESOLVED | Green — Responsible Team marked as resolved |
| CLOSED | Grey — Manager confirmed resolution and closed the ticket |
| REOPEN | Red — Employee or Manager reopened a resolved/closed complaint |

| 📘 Status Transition Rules OPEN → INPROCESS: only Manager can trigger (by assigning responsible_team).INPROCESS → ON HOLD / RESOLVED: only ResponsibleTeam can trigger.RESOLVED → CLOSED: only Manager can trigger.CLOSED → REOPEN: Employee or Manager can reopen; status resets to OPEN.ON HOLD → INPROCESS: only ResponsibleTeam can resume. |

chunks.h: Session 1 — Platform Setup & Account Management > Part D.1 — Team Groups: Bulk User Assignment > What Is a Team Group?
chunks.x:
Assigning one test user at a time (as done in Part D) works fine for training, but it does not scale. Real projects onboard users in batches — a new hire cohort, an entire department, or a partner organisation that all needs the same app access on day one. **Team Groups** (labelled **User collections**  inside the Workspace Hub screen) solve exactly this: they let you bundle a set of users once and assign the whole bundle to an application in a single step, instead of repeating the Part D steps per user.

Team Groups are of two kinds:

*
  **Individual Team Group** — created automatically for every user the moment their account is created. 	Hidden by default (use the **Show Individual** checkbox to reveal them). Its only job is to let a newly created app be auto-assigned back to the user who created it.
*
  **Group Team Group** — created manually 	by an admin, and the one you will use for real onboarding work. It 	holds any number of users and can be linked to one or more **App Collections** (App Groups) so that every user in the group inherits access to every app in the collection

**Why Team Groups Matter in Practice**

chunks.h: Session 1 — Platform Setup & Account Management > Part D.1 — Team Groups: Bulk User Assignment > What Is a Team Group?
chunks.x:
* Without Team Groups, assigning 25 new employees to 3 apps means 75 manual assignment actions (Part D, repeated).
* With a Team Group, it becomes: 1 group with 25 members, linked once to an App Collection with 3 apps.
* Team Groups are filtered by the logged-in user’s Auth Codes and scoped to the current landscape — you will only see groups you are authorised to manage.

The Customer Complaints BRD defines a ResponsibleTeam persona made up of several support agents, not just one test user. Rather than repeating Part D for each agent individually, model the onboarding the way a real project would:

| **Link to an App Collection**  | 	 	 Under the group’s App Groups tab, add the Customer Complaints App Collection so every member inherits the ResponsibleTeam role assignment.  |
| **Verify in bulk**   | 		 Log in as any one member. Confirm the app is visible, exactly as verified individually in Part D — but this time achieved through the group, not a per-user step.  |

For onboarding sets larger than a handful of users, Team Groups also support bulk **Excel upload/download**, so a spreadsheet of usernames can populate group membership without clicking through the UI one row at a time. This is the same mechanism used for App Collections and is the recommended approach once a group exceeds roughly 10–15 members.

🛠 **Hands-On — Try It Yourself**

* Export your grp_response_team_\ group to Excel.
* Add two more (fictional) usernames as new rows.
* Re-upload the file and confirm the new rows appear as pending/invalid members (since

  those users don’t yet exist) — this is expected and demonstrates the validation Procify performs on upload.

chunks.h: Session 1 — Platform Setup & Account Management > Part E —  understanding the importance of Procify
chunks.x:
Every application starts the same way: someone hands a developer a requirements document and says 'build this.' The Customer complaints Application Business Requirement Document (BRD) you read in Session 1 defines exactly what data needs to be stored — 3 data objects, their fields, and their relationships. The first job as a developer is to turn those definitions into a working database schema.

Before opening any tool, it is worth understanding what that process looks like — and how much of it Procify eliminates. The rest of this part walks through the traditional process step by step, then shows exactly which steps the data studio replaces.

chunks.h: Session 1 — Platform Setup & Account Management > What Is a Schema?
chunks.x: | 📘  Schema — The Blueprint of Your Application's Data A schema is the complete definition of the data your application stores: what tables exist, what columns each table has, what type of data each column holds, and how tables relate to each other. The schema is the foundation of every application. Without it, there is no database. Without a database, there is no data. Without data, there is no application. Building the schema is always the first development task after reading a BRD. Everything else — APIs, Pages, logic — is built on top of it. In our BRD, the schema is already defined in Section 4 (Entity Relationship Overview). The 4 entities, their properties, and their relationships are all there. Our job today is to implement that schema. |

chunks.h: Session 1 — Platform Setup & Account Management > The Traditional Way of Building a Schema
chunks.x: | 🏗  How developers build a schema without a low-code platform Step 1 — Write SQL scripts: A backend developer writes CREATE TABLE statements for each entity. For the Delivery table alone, that is 12 columns — each with its SQL data type, constraints, default values, and indexes. Step 2 — Write an ORM model: For every SQL table, the developer writes a model class in the backend language (Node.js/TypeScript, Python, Java). This class mirrors the database table and handles object-relational mapping. Step 3 — Write REST API endpoints: For each entity, the developer writes GET, POST, PUT, DELETE API handlers. Each handler validates input, maps it to the model, executes the database query, and returns the response. Step 4 — Write validation logic: For each property that has rules (mandatory, unique, min/max), the developer writes validation code — either in the model or in the API handler. Step 5 — Handle database migrations: Every time the schema changes (new property, renamed column), the developer writes a migration script to alter the existing tables without losing data. Step 6 — Test the API: The developer uses Postman or writes unit tests to verify each endpoint returns the correct data in the correct format. Repeat for all 4 entities. |

chunks.h: Session 1 — Platform Setup & Account Management > The Traditional Way of Building a Schema
chunks.x: | 🔴  The pain of the traditional approach Multiple files across multiple layers — SQL files, model files, API controller files, test files. A change to one field requires edits in 4–6 places. Context switching: a single developer must switch between SQL, backend language, API design, and test writing — each requiring a different mental mode. Time cost: 3–4 days of developer time before a single screen can be shown to a stakeholder. Repetition: most of this work is identical boilerplate — every entity needs the same pattern of SQL + ORM + CRUD APIs. Nothing creative, just repetitive. |

chunks.h: Session 1 — Platform Setup & Account Management > The Procify Way
chunks.x:
| ✅  How Procifyreplaces the traditional schema-building process In Klobase, all 6 traditional steps are replaced by a single tool: the data studio. You define the entity (name, type) → add properties (name, data type, key attributes) → click Update Schema. Done. The platform automatically generates: the database table (SQL step 1), the data access layer (ORM step 2), the REST API endpoints (step 3), basic validation from key attributes (step 4), and handles schema updates automatically (step 5). There are no separate files to keep in sync. The data studio is the single source of truth. Everything downstream — API, data validation, mobile sync — is derived from it automatically. Time with Klobase: the same 4 entities, all properties, schema live in the database — approximately 2 hours in this session. The developer's time is freed for the parts that actually require thinking: business logic, UI design, user experience. |

This is not an approximation. Let us make it concrete:

| Traditional Task | data studio Replacement |

chunks.h: Session 1 — Platform Setup & Account Management > The Procify Way
chunks.x:
| Write CREATE TABLE SQL for Delivery entity | Create entity in data studio — choose type, add properties, click Save |
| Write ORM model class (12 fields × 4 entities) | Already done — properties ARE the model |
| Write 16+ REST API endpoints | Already done — fireQuery apis are available to fetch data |
| Write validation for mandatory fields | Check the Mandatory key attribute icon on the property and validation will be handled by platform. |
| Write database migration script | Click Update Schema again — the platform handles ALTER TABLE automatically |
| Test APIs with Postman | Use the built-in Test function in the data studio toolbar |

chunks.h: Session 1 — Platform Setup & Account Management > The Procify Way > The Traditional Way of Building a UI
chunks.x: | 🔴 Traditional screen development requires five separate layers 1. HTML / JSX template — the visual structure: list container, card component, placeholder slots for each field. 2. CSS / styling — card appearance, status badge colours, spacing, responsiveness for mobile and desktop. 3. API call — GET /complaints?user={currentUser.id} to fetch complaint records from the server. 4. State management (React state, Redux, etc.) — store the fetched array, handle loading state, handle error state, trigger re-renders when data changes. 5. Data binding — map each complaint object's fields to the template slots: {complaint.complaint_desc}, {complaint.priority}. Total: 3–5 files, 150–300 lines of code, for one list screen. Any change to one layer often requires changes to the others. |

chunks.h: Session 1 — Platform Setup & Account Management > The Procify Way > The Procify Way — The Page Wizard & Page Builder
chunks.x: | ✅ The Page Builder replaces all five layers with a single metadata configuration In the Page Builder you configure the screen structure. The platform reads your configuration and generates the visual rendering, handles all data fetching, manages state automatically, applies your styling choices, and wires up the data bindings. This means: one tool, no files to keep in sync, no merge conflicts on screen structure, no state management code. The Page Wizard (used in this session) gives you a ready-made screen in minutes. Session 2 teaches you to build the same screen step-by-step so you understand every level of the hierarchy. Pages configured in the Page Builder render identically on both browser (web) and mobile (KloTouch) — no separate mobile codebase needed. |

chunks.h: Session 2 — BOL: Entity Fundamentals & Initial Pages > Part A — BOL Entity Fundamentals: Creating the Remaining Entities > A.1 — Business Object (BO) Hierarchy Explained
chunks.x:
A Business Object is a hierarchical tree of entities. The root entity represents the BO. Child entities are dependent on the root via Primary Relations. Standalone entities are linked via Non-Primary (Aggregated) Relations.

| 📘  BO Hierarchy — Customer Complaints d_complaints  (Root Entity / BO)  d_complaint_item  (Root Entity / BO)  d_complaint_voices     (Root Entity / BO)  d_complaints_attachment (Root Entity / BO) d_customers (Root Entity / BO)d_resp_team (Root Entity / BO) |

Primary Key (PK) — unique record identifier.
 Mandatory (❗) — field cannot be empty.
Unique Key — no duplicate values allowed.
Parent Key — auto-copies PK from parent entity into child on creation.

chunks.h: Session 2 — BOL: Entity Fundamentals & Initial Pages > Part B — Understanding Data Studio and Page Builder
chunks.x: Before building screens, every developer must be familiar with the two core design tools in Klobase: the Data Studio (BOL Editor) and the Page Builder (UI Editor). This part gives you an orientation of both tools and their layouts, then walks through building the Customer Complaints screen step by step — showing the expected output at each stage.

chunks.h: Session 2 — BOL: Entity Fundamentals & Initial Pages > Part B — Understanding Data Studio and Page Builder > B.1 — Data Studio (BOL Editor) — Tool Layout
chunks.x:
Navigate to Design Studio → Data Studio. The editor is divided into two major sections: the Tree on the left and the Detail on the right.

| Section | What It Does |

| **Tree (Left)** | Lists all entities, queries, and value helps in the selected app. Click any item to load it in the Detail panel. Use Expand All / Collapse All to navigate. Use the search bar to find entities quickly. |
| **Detail (Right)** | Shows all configuration tabs for the selected object: Properties, Relations, Object Type, Status, Queries, Rules, Entity Index. Only visible when an item is selected from the tree. |
| **Toolbar (Top)** | Context-sensitive: Save, Edit, Update Schema, Validate, Delete, Test, Metadata File. Actions change depending on what is selected in the tree. |
| **App Selector** | Dropdown at the top-left to switch between your assigned apps. Always verify the correct app is selected before making any changes. |
| **Normal / Expert Mode** | Toggle in the toolbar. Normal Mode: Entity, Query, Value Help creation. Expert Mode: adds Status Config, Object Group Config, Entity Index. Expert Mode needed from Session 3 onwards. Note: Currently there is no difference between expert mode and normal mode |

chunks.h: Session 2 — BOL: Entity Fundamentals & Initial Pages > Part B — Understanding Data Studio and Page Builder > B.1 — Data Studio (BOL Editor) — Tool Layout
chunks.x: | 📘  Data Studio Reference Source: BOL Editor 7.0 User Guide — Sections 2.0 Editor Sections, 1.4 Modes Tree: expand, collapse, filter — same panel used for all entity operations. Detail panel tabs depend on context: entity selected shows Properties/Relations/Status; query shows query config. Update Schema: converts entity metadata into actual DB table. Required after every property change. Test button: opens the Data Browser for CRUD operations on the entity directly from the editor. |

chunks.h: Session 2 — BOL: Entity Fundamentals & Initial Pages > Part B — Understanding Data Studio and Page Builder > B.2 — Page Builder (UI Editor) — Tool Layout
chunks.x:
Navigate to Design Studio → Page Builder. According to the UI Editor 7.0 User Guide, the editor is divided into four major sections:

| Section | What It Does |

| **Tree (Left)** | Hierarchical view of the entire page structure: Page → Page Layout → Page Area → Section → Controls. All creation, renaming, and assignment is done via right-click context menu in this tree. |
| **Preview (Centre)** | Live render of the screen. Refreshes on Save. Use the Auto Refresh toggle for real-time updates. Full Preview loads actual data from the database for testing. |
| **Detail (Down)** | Configuration panel for the selected tree element. Shows different properties depending on whether you have selected a Page, Page Layout, Page Area, Section, or Control. |
| **Page Data Model (Right — Tab)** | TransNode configuration. Defines what data is available to the page. Use the + button to add Model Paths. Each TransNode has: an ID, an Entity/Query binding, a Node Type (EntitySet / Entity / Query), and an optional Fold From parent. |

chunks.h: Session 2 — BOL: Entity Fundamentals & Initial Pages > Part B — Understanding Data Studio and Page Builder > B.2 — Page Builder (UI Editor) — Tool Layout
chunks.x:
| 📘  Page Builder Toolbar Reference (UI Editor 7.0 User Guide — Section 1.0) Edit icon — enables edit mode on the tree. You MUST click this before creating or renaming anything. + icon — create a new page (blank or from wizard). Save icon — commits all pending changes. Required before preview refreshes. Show Full Preview — loads real database records into the preview for testing. Detail icon — toggles visibility of the detail properties panel. Page Data Model icon — toggles visibility of the TransNode / data model panel. Reset Perspective — restores all panels to their default size and position. Preview In — switch preview between desktop, tablet, and mobile device views. |

Every screen in Klobase follows a strict 5-level hierarchy. This is the most important structural concept in UI development. Each level has a mandatory naming convention prefix:

chunks.h: Session 2 — BOL: Entity Fundamentals & Initial Pages > Part B — Understanding Data Studio and Page Builder > B.3 — The Page Hierarchy (UI Editor 7.0 User Guide — Sections 3.0–7.0)
chunks.x: | 📘  Five-Level Page Hierarchy Level 1 — PAGE (prefix: p_)     The root container. Holds all layouts. Created first. One page can have multiple layouts (one per device type).     At runtime, the platform picks the layout based on device: screencontainerdesktop, screencontainermobile, screencontainertab, screencontainerdefault.     Level 2 — PAGE LAYOUT (prefix: pl_)     Sits directly under the Page. Defines HOW the page areas are arranged.     screenType options: stack, tab, two_column, object_page, grid_layout, hsplitter, vsplitter.     Example: pl_complaints_desk (two column layout for desktop).          Level 3 — PAGE AREA (prefix: pa_)          A logical sub-container inside the layout. Can itself have a screenType (tab, stack, splitter).          Sections are assigned to page areas to determine WHERE they render.          Example: pa_complaints (list area), pa_complaint_details (detail area).               Level 4 — SECTION (prefix: s_)               The rendering unit. screenType determines HOW it displays data.               Types: search, cardlist, card, form, grid, tree, timeline, map, calendar.               Must be assigned to a Page Area to appear in the UI.               Example: s_search (search), s_complaints (grid), s_detail_header (form).                    Level 5 — CONTROLS                    Individual fields, buttons, labels, icons bound to entity properties.                    Added via: right-click section → New → Controls, OR drag from unused TransNode properties. |

chunks.h: Session 2 — BOL: Entity Fundamentals & Initial Pages > Part B — Understanding Data Studio and Page Builder > B.3 — The Page Hierarchy (UI Editor 7.0 User Guide — Sections 3.0–7.0)
chunks.x:
| Section screenType | Renders As |

| **search** | Filter bar with Close / Reset / Search buttons. Auto-generates the search toolbar. |
| **cardlist** | List of records as card rows — one card per record. Good for mobile and compact lists. |
| **grid** | Tabular list with column headers and rows. Supports sort, filter, group-by per column. |
| **form** | Detail form layout. Each control renders as a labelled input field. |
| **card** | Single entity rendered as a CSS grid card. One record only. |
| **tab** | Used on Page Areas to group child sections as tabs. showTitle must be true for tab labels. |
| **tree** | Hierarchical tree display for nested data. |

chunks.h: Session 2 — BOL: Entity Fundamentals & Initial Pages > Part B — Understanding Data Studio and Page Builder > B.4 — Page Data Model (TransNodes) — Concept
chunks.x:
The Page Data Model defines the data available to a screen. Every section and control that displays data must be bound to a TransNode. A TransNode is a “data pipe” — it fetches entity records from the database and makes them available to sections and controls on the page.

| Node Type | Fetches |

| **EntitySet** | A LIST of records. Use for search sections, grids, card lists. Suffix convention: _list. Example: d_complaints_list |
| **Entity** | ONE record (the currently selected record). Use for detail forms. Suffix convention: _detail. Example: d_complaints_detail |
| **Query** | Records from a kloQuery with WHERE conditions, joins, sorting. Suffix convention: _query. |
| **Other** | Non-standard / custom use cases. |

| 📘  Fold From — The Critical Link Between List and Detail When you create d_complaints_detail (Entity type) and set its “Fold From” \= d_complaints_list, the platform automatically loads the selected record’s data into d_complaints_detail whenever the user clicks a row in the list. This is the mechanism that connects list → detail. Without Fold From: the detail section will always be empty. With Fold From: clicking any complaint row in the list instantly populates the detail form. TransNode naming convention (from UI Editor 7.0 Guide):   EntitySet → _list suffix    Entity → _detail suffix    Query → _query suffix |

chunks.h: Session 2 — BOL: Entity Fundamentals & Initial Pages > Session 3 — Entity Configuration (Relations, Object Types, Status, ID Series) > A.1 — What Is an Entity Relation?
chunks.x:
An Entity Relation tells the Klobase server how two entities are connected to each other. Without a relation defined in the BOL Editor, the platform has no way to automatically load child records when a parent record is selected — and no way to bundle the BO for save/delete operations.

There are two types of relations in Klobase:

| Relation Type | What It Means |

| Primary Relation | Tight parent-child bond WITHIN the same Business Object (BO). A child entity is dependent on the parent. Prefixed pr_. Used for d_complaint_item, d_complaint_voices, d_complaints_attachment — all children of d_complaints. |
| Non-Primary (Aggregated) Relation | Looser link BETWEEN BOs. Used to reference standalone master entities. Prefixed r_. Used for d_customers and d_resp_team which are independent master entities. |

| 📘  Why Relations Matter in the UI |

chunks.h: Session 2 — BOL: Entity Fundamentals & Initial Pages > Session 3 — Entity Configuration (Relations, Object Types, Status, ID Series) > A.1 — What Is an Entity Relation?
chunks.x:
| When a relation is defined and referenced in a TransNode in the Page Builder, the platform automatically fetches the child/linked entity records when the parent record is loaded. |
| Without a relation, you would have to write manual queries and wire up the data fetch yourself. |
| The TransNode type 'Relation' in the Page Data Model uses the relation name defined here — this is why naming the relation correctly matters. |
| Naming convention (from BOL Editor 7.0 User Guide — Best Practices): pr_ prefix for primary relations, r_ prefix for associated/aggregated relations. Always lowercase. |

chunks.h: Session 2 — BOL: Entity Fundamentals & Initial Pages > Session 3 — Entity Configuration (Relations, Object Types, Status, ID Series) > B.1 — What Is an Object Type?
chunks.x:
In Klobase, an Object Type (stored in the system property `s_object_type`) is a classification that tags each record as belonging to a specific type. Object Types serve two important purposes:

* They enable role-based visibility: a button or field can be made visible/editable only for a specific role **AND** a specific object type combination. This is used for screen behavior in Session 7.
* They allow ID Series to be object-type-specific: a different number series prefix can be applied per object type — for example, complaints created by Maventic employees might use a different prefix than those created by Procify employees.

| 📘  Object Type vs Object Group |

| **Object Group** is a container that groups related Object Types together. The group is used as the filter boundary. **Object Type** is the actual tag applied to individual records (e.g. MAVENTIC, PROCIFY). Every Object Type must belong to exactly one Object Group. For the Customer Complaints application: Object Group \= `company_types` Object Types \= `MAVENTIC`, `PROCIFY` **Best Practice (BOL Editor 7.0 User Guide):** Always maintain an Object Group to group types — the same group can be used in default filters based on users. |
|  |

| Object Type ID | Description |

| MAVENTIC | Complaints created by Maventic employees |
| PROCIFY | Complaints created by Procify employees |

chunks.x:
An ID Series is a platform-managed counter that automatically generates primary key values when a new record is created. Without an ID Series on complaint_id, a developer would need to generate unique IDs manually — which is error-prone and cannot produce readable, formatted numbers like CMP-00001.

| ID Series Type | Description |

| Auto Number | Returns an incrementing number. Combined with a Prefix pattern to produce CMP-00001, CMP-00002, etc. |
| GUID | Returns a 32-character UUID. Good for distributed offline scenarios. Not human-readable. |
| None | No auto-generation. The developer or rule must set the key manually. |

| Property | Type | Company | Pattern/Prefix | Start From |

| complaint_id | Auto Number | PROCIFY | Prefix: P- (generates P-00001) | 1 |
| complaint_id | Auto Number | MAVENTIC | Prefix: M - (generates M-00001) | 1 |

chunks.h: Session 2 — BOL: Entity Fundamentals & Initial Pages > Session 3 — Entity Configuration (Relations, Object Types, Status, ID Series) > C.1 — What Is Status in Klobase?
chunks.x:
The system property s_status represents the current state of a complaint record. The Status tab in the Data Studio lets you define the allowed values for s_status and group them into Status Groups.

Status Groups are named collections of statuses. They are used in Vienable (Session 7) to control screen behaviour: for example, the Edit button is visible only when s_status is in the OPEN_GROUP, and the Assign Team button is visible only when s_status is in the INPROCESS_GROUP.

| 📘  Status Lifecycle for Customer Complaints |

| The complaint lifecycle defined in the BRD has 6 states: |
| OPEN → INPROCESS → ON_HOLD / RESOLVED → CLOSED / REOPEN |
| Each status transition is triggered by a specific role (defined in the Role Responsibility matrix from Session 1 Part A). |
| In this session you define the status values and groups. The actual UI enforcement of transitions using Vienable happens in Session 7. |
|  |

| CLOSED | Closed | COMPLETED | Manager confirms resolution and closes |
| REOPEN | Re-Opened | OPEN | Employee or Manager reopens a closed complaint |

chunks.h: Quick Reference > Session 4 — Value Helps & Queries > A.1 — What Is a Value Help?
chunks.x:
A Value Help (VH) is a platform-level component that provides a controlled list of choices for an entity property. When a VH is assigned to a property, the corresponding input field in the UI automatically renders as a dropdown (ComboBox), auto-complete field, or picker dialog (F4) — without any additional coding. The VH also validates that the entered value exists in the list when 'Is Restricted' is enabled.

| 📘  Three VH Types in Klobase (VH User Guide — Section 1.1) |

| VH Config: Values are maintained in the metadata (config) DB. App-managed, flavor-dependent. Can be overridden by child apps. Requires a build after creation/update. Use for fixed classification lists (priority, complaint_type, etc.). |
| VH Query: Values are fetched from a transactional or modelled query at runtime. Use for dynamic master data pickers (customer_id, responsible_team). The query determines what data appears in the picker. |
| VH Transaction (DEPRECATED): Older type. Internally still supported for legacy apps. New development should use VH Config or VH Query instead. |
|  |

| VH Type | Source | Naming | Use Case for This App |

| VH Config | Metadata / Config DB | vhc_\ | priority, complaint_type, nature_of_complaint |
| VH Query | Transactional / Modelled Query | vhq_\ | customer_id → d_customers, responsible_team → d_resp_team |

chunks.h: Quick Reference > Session 4 — Value Helps & Queries > C.1 — What Is VH Query?
chunks.x:
A VH Query fetches its suggestion items from a live entity or modelled query at runtime. Unlike VH Config (which is static metadata), VH Query shows records that are currently in the transactional database. This is the right choice for master entity pickers — where the data comes from d_customers, d_resp_team, or any other entity that can be searched and selected.

| Entity/Query: The entity name or modelled query ID that returns the list of suggestions. |
| Key Property: The property whose value gets STORED in the parent entity when the user selects an item. For d_customers → customer_id. |

| Desc Format: How the display appears. Example: :customer_id--:customer_name shows ID followed by Name. |
| Icon: Optional — entity property that holds an icon URL to show alongside each suggestion item. |

chunks.h: Quick Reference > Session 4 — Value Helps & Queries > D.1 — What Is a KloQuery?
chunks.x:
A KloQuery is the Klobase equivalent of a SQL SELECT statement. It lets you define — within the Data Studio — exactly what records to fetch, from which entity, with which filters, joins, and sort order. Unlike a Runtime Entity Query (which simply fetches all records of an entity), a Modelled Query gives you full control over the WHERE clause, JOIN entities, and sort order — and is reusable across multiple pages.

| Query Type | When to Use |

| Runtime Query (Entity Query) | Fetch all records of a single entity. No WHERE clause in the definition. Filters applied at runtime via the TransNode. Use for simple list screens. |
| Modelled Query (Dynamic Query) | Define custom WHERE conditions, joins, sort order in the BOL Editor. Reusable, entity-independent. Use for role-filtered lists (My Complaints), VH Queries backed by joins, aggregated results. |
| Native Query (Advanced Query) | Raw SQL. Database-specific. Use only for special cases not achievable with modelled queries. Avoid training. |

| 📘  KloQuery Fields Reference (BOL Editor 7.0 User Guide — Section 3.0.2) |

chunks.h: Quick Reference > Session 4 — Value Helps & Queries > D.1 — What Is a KloQuery?
chunks.x:
| Return Entity: The entity whose properties appear in the result set. |
| Query Type: Runtime | Modelled | Native — affects which tabs are available. |
| Entities And Join: Add the root entity and any joined entities (LEFT JOIN, INNER JOIN, etc.). |
| Select Properties: Choose which properties from the entities appear in the result. |
| Parameters: Define input parameters the query accepts at runtime (e.g., user_id filter passed from the TransNode). |
| Where: Define filter conditions: entity.property \= :parameter or entity.property \= 'fixed_value'. |
| Sort Order: Set the default sorting column and direction (ASC / DESC). |
| Naming convention: Query IDs must start with q_. All lowercase. |

chunks.h: Quick Reference > Session 4 — Value Helps & Queries > E.1 — What Is a Saved Query?
chunks.x:
A Saved Query is a named combination of a base query and a specific set of pre-filled search parameters. Where a Modelled Query defines the structure, a Saved Query defines a pre-configured instance of that query — ready to execute with one click in the search bar. Saved Queries appear as quick-filter options in the search TransNode of the UI.

| 📘  Saved Query vs Modelled Query (Basic Training Guide — Section 2.1) |

| Modelled Query: The definition — entity, properties, parameters, WHERE logic. Reusable structure. |
| Saved Query: A named configuration of a modelled query with preset parameter values. Stored per entity. |
| In the UI, a Saved Query appears as a quick-filter button or dropdown in the search bar section. |
| Saved Queries are created from the Data Browser (Advanced Search), not directly in the query detail tab. |
| Naming convention for Saved Query IDs: Begin with sq_ by convention. |
|  |

chunks.x:
The entity .ts file for d_complaints is located in the Private Node workspace at the path:

| workspace/apps/\/d_complaints.ts |

If the file does not exist yet, the private node can generate it. The base structure looks like this:

| import { KloEntity, ValidationError, ErrorType } from 'klobase'; export class d_complaints extends KloEntity {   // ── Getters & Setters ──────────────────────────────────────────   // ── Lifecycle Hooks ────────────────────────────────────────────   public async onAfterCreate(): Promise\ {     // Called after a new complaint record is created   }   public async OnValidate(): Promise\ {     // Called during navigation if transnode setActiveIf \= Valid   }   public async onDelete(): Promise\ {     // Called after the record is deleted   } } |

| 💡  Architecture Principle: Business Logic Belongs Here |

| The entity file is the authoritative location for all business logic. Period. |
| Controller file → UI orchestration only (navigation, formatter functions, show/hide decisions). |
| Entity file → field defaults, cross-field computations, validations, role enforcement. |
| Never duplicate validation logic in the controller. If the controller calls commitP(), OnValidate() fires automatically on the server — that is your safety net. |
| Reference: kloTouch 7.0 Basic Training Guide — Section 7.5 Best Practice Do's and Don'ts (Entity File). |
|  |

chunks.h: Quick Reference > Session 5 — BOL Logic & Validations with dashboard creation > B.1 — The Three Hook Methods
chunks.x:
Klobase provides three entity lifecycle hook methods that you override in the entity .ts file. These run on the server and are triggered automatically by the platform at the appropriate point in the entity's lifecycle.

| Method | When Called | Trigger Condition | Primary Use |

| onAfterCreate() | After entity is created in DB | On every new entity save | Set defaults, auto-populate audit fields, initialise related records |
| OnValidate() | During navigation / on save / validateP function | TransNode setActiveIf \= 'Valid' | Validate field values, enforce business rules, push errors |
| onDelete() | After entity is deleted | On every delete operation | Cascade cleanup, logging, send notifications |

| 📘  OnValidate — Important Details  |

chunks.h: Quick Reference > Session 5 — BOL Logic & Validations with dashboard creation > B.1 — The Three Hook Methods
chunks.x:
| OnValidate is triggered ONLY when the TransNode's 'setActiveIf' property is set to 'Valid' in the Page Builder. |
| If setActiveIf is not set, OnValidate does NOT fire — the platform skips validation on navigation. |
| Inside OnValidate, push errors using: this.errors.push(new ValidationError(this, propertyId, errorCode, message, ErrorType.ERROR)); |
| The method must NOT return the errors array — it pushes to this.errors and the platform reads it. (PROC-24075 fixed this for proper return type.) |
| ErrorType.ERROR blocks save. ErrorType.WARNING allows save but shows a warning toast. |
| After your OnValidate runs, the platform ALSO runs its own mandatory-field validation based on key attributes — you don't need to repeat those. |
|  |

chunks.h: Quick Reference > Session 5 — BOL Logic & Validations with dashboard creation > C.1 — What are Entity Rules?
chunks.x:
Rules contain business logic codes. It works with the event bus, any change in the entity will trigger the event, and all the rules hooked with the event will be executed sequentially. Rules are reusable objects across client, server and middleware.

EX:

1. When a complaint is created  by an employee then status should be OPEN and assigned_to should be the same user.
2. A responsible team/manager/assigned_to can be assigned by the manager only.
3. An employee or manager can delete the complaint but not the responsible team

| Field | Default Value Logic |

| s_status | 'OPEN' — every new complaint starts in OPEN status |
| assigned_to | this.txn.getUserID() — auto-set to the logged-in user who created the complaint |
| created_on | this.s_created_on — already auto-set by system field, no action needed |
| created_by | this.s_created_by — already auto-set by system field, no action needed |

chunks.h: Quick Reference > Session 5 — BOL Logic & Validations with dashboard creation > D.1 — What Are Setters and Getters?
chunks.x:
TypeScript property accessors let you intercept reads and writes of entity properties. In Klobase, setters and getters in the entity .ts file are the correct place for computed/derived field logic — not the controller.

| Pattern | Purpose |

| Setter (set propertyId) | Called every time the property value changes. Use to: compute a derived field when an input changes, enforce value formatting, trigger side-effects. |
| Getter (get propertyId) | Called every time the property value is read. Use to: return a computed / formatted value instead of the raw stored value. |

| ⚠  Critical Setter Pattern — Always Call this.s() |

| Inside a setter, you MUST call this.s('propertyId', new_value, 'dataType', false, false) to actually persist the new value into the entity's internal state. |
| Without this.s(), the new_value is accepted by TypeScript but never written to the entity data — the save will ignore your change. |
| Pattern: if(new_value \== this.propertyId) return;  // guard to avoid infinite loop |
| Then: this.s('propertyId', new_value, 'dataType', false, false); |
|  |

| public set closed_on(new_value: Date) {   if (new_value \== this.closed_on) return;   this.s('closed_on', new_value, 'date', false, false);   // Compute actual_tat when closed_on is set   if (new_value && this.s_created_on) {     const msPerDay \= 1000 * 60 * 60 * 24;     const diffMs \= new Date(new_value).getTime() - new Date(this.s_created_on).getTime();     this.actual_tat \= parseFloat((diffMs / msPerDay).toFixed(1));   } } |

Part E — Query Rules

**E.1 — What are Query Rules?**

chunks.h: Quick Reference > Session 5 — BOL Logic & Validations with dashboard creation > E.4 — Testing OnValidate
chunks.x:
`Query rules are similar to Entity rules but are triggered before and after a query execution rather than around a create/update/delete. They are the correct place to answer two very different questions:

1. **Before the database is asked anything** — “what should this user even be allowed to see?” (row-level filtering, defaulting search criteria).
2.  **After the database has answered** — “does the raw result need reshaping before it reaches the client?” 	(adding computed fields, merging data from a second query, masking sensitive values, sorting/aggregating in ways the query modeller can’t express.

Both callbacks receive an EventContext (commonly named oEvent) and give access to the query instance itself via oEvent.getObject().

**E.1 — How to Create Query Rules?**

Creating query rules is the same as creating entity rules, except the event type you subscribe to is one of:

**Event types:**

* **Before Query** (beforeQ) — executes before the query is fired against the database. 	Anything set on the query object here becomes part of the WHERE condition.
* **After Query** (afterQ) 	— executes after results come back from the database, before they are returned to the client. The raw result set can be read and replaced here.

**Query Rule Event Reference (BOL API)**

chunks.h: Quick Reference > Session 5 — BOL Logic & Validations with dashboard creation > E.4 — Testing OnValidate
chunks.x:
* Event.getObject() — returns the KloQueryForRule instance being executed. Set properties on it to add filter conditions (beforeQ), or call getResults() / setResults() on it to read/replace the raw result rows (afterQ).
* Event.getTxn() — returns the KloTransaction for the current user; use it to read \$SYSTEM.roleID, call this.txn.get\$User(), or check permissions.
* Event.getEventType() — returns which event fired, e.g. BEFORE_QUERY or AFTER_QUERY. Useful if one method is wired to handle both events.

queryInstance.getResults() / setResults() — read or replace the raw JSON array of result rows in an afterQ callback. These are plain objects, not KloEntity instances — they cannot be saved back.

chunks.h: Quick Reference > Session 6 — Bindings, Navigation & Styling > Part A — Data Bindings In Depth
chunks.x: Every control on a Klobase screen reads and writes data through the Transaction Model (\$M). The model is a JSON model object. All bindings use the prefix \$M to reference it. Without a binding, a control shows a static value or nothing at all — it is disconnected from the live data.

chunks.h: Quick Reference > Session 6 — Bindings, Navigation & Styling > Part A — Data Bindings In Depth > A.1 — The \$M Model Path Structure
chunks.x:
The Transaction Model is organized as a tree. Each TransNode in the Page Data Model corresponds to a branch in the \$M tree. The full path to any property follows this pattern:

`{$M>/transNodeRelationId/propertyId}`

For a list TransNode with relationId \= list, the first row's complaint_desc is:

`{\$M>/list/0/complaint_desc}`

For the detail TransNode with relationId \= detail:

`{\$M>/detail/complaint_desc}`

The leading / after > is mandatory. Omitting it causes a silent bind failure.

chunks.h: Quick Reference > Session 6 — Bindings, Navigation & Styling > Part A — Data Bindings In Depth > A.2 — The Four Binding Modes
chunks.x:
| Mode | When to Use | Syntax / Where to Set | Example |

| Value | Static, hardcoded value — no model connection. Control always shows this literal text regardless of data. | Properties tab → Value field | text \= 'Complaint ID' — always shows that label. |
| Path | Bind to exactly ONE model property. Two-way binding by default: changes in UI write back to model. | Properties tab → DSRC field | {\$M>/detail/complaint_desc} — shows and edits the complaint description. |
| Parts | Combine MULTIPLE paths into one display value via a formatter function. Always one-way (read only). | Properties tab → dsrc field (add each path as a part) + Formatter Function field | Parts: {\$M>/detail/first_name} + {\$M>/detail/last_name} → formatter returns full name string. |
| Expression | Inline calculated value. No formatter function needed. Supports ternary operators and comparisons. Always one-way. | Properties tab → dsrc field (starts with {= ...}) | {= \${\$M>/detail/is_escalated} \=== true ? 'Escalated' : 'Normal'} |

⚠  Path and Parts are mutually exclusive on the same property — you cannot use both at once. If you need multiple values combined, always use Parts.

chunks.h: Part A — Vienable: Complete Configuration Guide
chunks.x: Vienable (Visible + Enable) is the declarative system for controlling control visibility and editability across four independent dimensions. The final result for any control is the intersection of all configured dimensions: a control is visible only if ALL applicable dimension rules say it should be visible.

chunks.h: Part A — Vienable: Complete Configuration Guide > A.1 — The Four Vienable Dimensions
chunks.x:
| Dimension | What It Controls | Values | Configuration Location |

| Page Size | Visibility/enable by device screen resolution. Evaluated based on the PARENT section's resolved size. | S (phone), M (tablet), L (desktop), XL (wide desktop) | Vienable Dashboard → Page Size columns: S, M, L, XL |
| Page Mode | Visibility/enable by current screen interaction mode. Default mode is DISPLAY. | Display, Edit, Create, Review | Vienable Dashboard → Page Mode columns |
| Role | Visibility/enable by the logged-in user's s_role_rollup value. Config must be maintained in BOL Editor → Object Type tab. | Owner (10), Supervisor (20), Reviewer (30), Overlooker (40). In this app: EMPLOYEE=10, EMPLOYEE_MANAGER=20, IT_TEAM=30 | Vienable Dashboard → Role column |
| Status Group | Visibility/enable by the bound entity's current s_status_group value. Config must be maintained in BOL Editor → Status tab. | The Status Groups you defined in Session 3. In this app: OPEN, INPROCESS, ACCEPTED, COMPLETED | Vienable Dashboard → Status Group column |

⚠  Entity must be set to TRUE for the control row in the Vienable Dashboard. If Entity \= false, Role and Status Group dimensions are ignored — the control will always be visible/enabled regardless of role or status.
